1:
Luke fixes the moment by naming a man who is somewhere else. reformed John Gill notes that Apollos had come to Corinth after Paul and was watering there what Paul had planted, becoming so eminent that a party was set up in his name against the chief of the apostles — though Gill is careful to add that this was against his own will (1 Corinthians 1:12). puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the division of labour the point: while Apollos was watering at Corinth, Paul was planting at Ephesus, and Paul grudged not that Apollos had entered into his labours and was building on his foundation, but rejoiced in it, and went at the new work cut out for him with the more cheerfulness because he knew so able a minister was carrying on the good work behind him.

The route matters to the grammatical-historical witnesses more than to anyone else, and they read it off one word. Albert Barnes explains that the upper coasts are the higher regions of the interior — Phrygia and Galatia — called upper because they lie on the high table-land, while Ephesus stood in the low maritime country. Charles Ellicott adds the caution a modern reader needs: the coast in our sense of the word Paul did not so much as approach. A.T. Robertson takes the term as a late form meaning the highlands, and draws the practical inference — Paul did not take the usual Roman road west through Colossae and Laodicea in the Lycus valley, cities he had not visited (Colossians 2:1), but the more direct road down the Cayster valley. wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lists the same inland provinces and reports a variant: the Codex Bezae opens the chapter with Paul desiring to go to Jerusalem and the Spirit commanding him to return into Asia — a reading also in that manuscript's Latin column and in the margin of the later Syriac. John Wesley states the geography in a line and leaves it.

Robertson stops to describe the place Paul is arriving at, because the rest of the chapter depends on it. Asia here means the western part of Asia Minor, a senatorial province and a jewel of the empire, thick with great cities — Smyrna, Pergamum, Sardis, Laodicea, Colossae, Hierapolis among them. Ephesus was its capital, richer and larger than Corinth, standing at the entrance to the Maeander valley, where the power of Rome, the splendour of Greek culture and the full tide of oriental superstition and magic met. Henry names the same city by its temple to Diana, one of the wonders of the world; Robertson calls that temple by its Greek name and says the same thing of it.

Who the certain disciples were is the first real question of the chapter, and the witnesses divide. Henry places them in the lowest form of Christ's school, under his usher John the Baptist, and notes they were much of the standing Apollos himself had been of on arrival (Acts 18:25), only without his opportunity of being taught more perfectly by Aquila and Priscilla. Barnes agrees that they were in the same situation as Apollos, and adds that it is not even clear they had heard the Messiah had come. Robertson denies the connection outright: they show no link with Priscilla and Aquila, Apollos had already left, and they are better taken as floating followers of the Baptist who had drifted into Ephesus. Calvin declines to say whether they were residents or strangers and thinks it does not much matter, but holds it beyond doubt that they were Jews, since they had received John's baptism.
2:
Paul's question is not about conversion, and every witness says so before saying anything else. Gill distinguishes the special regenerating and sanctifying grace of the Spirit — which is presupposed in men already called disciples and believers — from the extraordinary gifts, which is what the question asks after. Barnes puts the reasoning as Paul would have had it: he would not doubt that men who had believed had received the ordinary converting influence, that being one of his own favourite doctrines; but the miraculous influences of the Spirit were conferred on most societies of believers as an evidence of God's presence and of their acceptance with him, and it was natural to ask whether that evidence had been granted here. Wesley says the same in a phrase, and Calvin argues it from the end of the story — the special gifts given at the beginning of the gospel for the common edifying of the Church.

Ellicott alters the translation and with it the sense of the whole exchange: better did ye receive the Holy Ghost when ye believed?, connecting the two facts in English as the Greek connects them, so that the question is about their conversion and baptism rather than about some later stage. What prompted it is left to conjecture, and Ellicott's guess is a pastoral one — that Paul noticed in them, as they attended the meetings of the church, an absence of spiritual gifts and perhaps of the peace and brightness that showed in others. They had the outward marks of a rigorous asceticism, the signs of repentance and mortification, but had not passed on to righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Ghost (Romans 14:17). Robertson reads the same suspicion off the encounter more bluntly, saying Paul was suspicious of the look or the conduct of these professed disciples, and notes the Greek particle used in a direct question — an idiom foreign to older Greek but common enough in the Septuagint and the New Testament.

The answer is the difficulty, and nobody takes it at face value. Clarke insists they cannot have meant that they had never heard of the Holy Spirit at all, since John himself announced the coming one as he who should baptize with the Holy Ghost (Matthew 3:11; Luke 3:16); what they meant was that they had not heard that the Spirit, in his gifts, had been given to or received by anyone. Ellicott says they must have known the Spirit as a name met in the sacred books and given to the prophets of old, but did not think of him as a living and pervading presence in which they might themselves claim a share. Calvin presses the impossibility hardest, asking how men who were Jews could have heard nothing of a Spirit of whom the prophets speak everywhere, and concludes that a figure of speech is at work in the wording; had they truly denied all knowledge of the Spirit, he says, Paul would never have passed over in silence an error so monstrous. Robertson is content to call it plain proof that they knew John's message poorly, and Barnes turns it to the reader's account: God may work important changes in men who have no clear or systematic views, and the mark of such a case is exactly what shows here — a readiness of heart to embrace the truth as soon as it is made known.

Clarke offers the one biographical guess in the group, that these were Asiatic Jews who had been at Jerusalem some twenty-six years earlier, had heard the Baptist preach and received his baptism, and had got no further instruction since.
3:
Paul's second question follows from the first as an inference rather than a change of subject. Gill sets out its logic: the apostle takes their baptism for granted, since they are not merely believers but disciples, men who have professed their faith and follow Christ; what he asks is what that baptism was — either in whose name it was administered, Christian baptism being in the name of the Spirit as well as of the Father and of the Son, or what attended and followed it, the Spirit having sometimes fallen on persons before baptism, sometimes at it, and sometimes after. Barnes reads the question more simply as asking what faith or doctrine they had professed when they were baptized.

Robertson works on the preposition. The phrase is better rendered unto what or on what basis, and he draws the same conclusion Paul evidently drew: they had been dipped, but they had not grasped the significance of the ordinance, and Paul plainly felt theirs was a poor baptism, made with no knowledge of the Holy Spirit. Wesley opens the question out into two: into what dispensation, and to the sealing of what doctrine?

Ellicott treats the exchange as a diagnosis reaching its conclusion. The previous answer had shown two defects at once — an instruction falling short of what catechumens ordinarily received before they were admitted to the new birth by water and the Spirit, and a spiritual experience to match. That raised the question whether men in such a state could have been admitted into the Church of Christ by baptism in his name at all; and the reply settles their position precisely. They were practically disciples of the Baptist, believing in Jesus as the Christ, and supposing that this by itself qualified them for communion with the Church of Christ.

Their answer names John, and Robertson marks the moment as a closing of a door: this is the last mention of John the Baptist in the New Testament. What follows is Paul explaining what John had actually been for, and it is fitting that the Baptist's last appearance in the record should be an explanation of his own provisional office.
4:
Paul's reply is not a correction of John but an unfolding of him, and the witnesses are unanimous on that point even where they differ about what follows from it. Gill reads it as an argument that John's baptism was agreeable to, and indeed the same in substance with, the baptism of Christ, being administered with respect to his name. Barnes gives the two halves of the sentence their weight: the baptism had special relation to repentance, or was a profession that the baptized did repent of their sins; and the design of John's coming was to turn the people from those sins and prepare them for the Messiah, so that he directed their attention principally to the one who was to come. Clarke isolates what was peculiar in it. The baptism of repentance was common to all the baptisms the Jews administered to proselytes; telling men that they should believe on him who was coming was John's own.

Ellicott takes the verse as the summary of a much fuller teaching, and finds the distinctive point in John's own declaration that his baptism was provisional and preparatory. He taught his disciples to believe in Jesus; belief implied obedience, and obedience implied baptism in his name. Ellicott adds an observation about the audience that is worth weighing: the list of elementary doctrines at the opening of the sixth chapter of Hebrews reads like what men in this condition would have learnt in their spiritual childhood, before the writer passes on to those who have been illumined and made partakers of the Holy Ghost (Hebrews 6:4-6).

Robertson supplies the grammar and then the sting. The genitive describes the baptism as marked by repentance rather than as conveying it — that being the work of the Holy Spirit — and John had also preached the baptism of the Holy Spirit which the Messiah was to bring; so if these men knew nothing of the Spirit, they had missed the point of John's baptism entirely. He notes that the phrase Paul uses, the one coming after me, is John's own identical wording as the Gospels report it, and doubts whether these disciples had believed in a Messiah at all, least of all in Jesus. Yet he refuses the conclusion that would be easiest: Paul does not mean that John's baptism was inadequate, but simply explains what John taught and therefore what his baptism signified.

Calvin turns the whole into a summons forward. Paul's admonition tended to this, that men convicted of their ignorance might desire to go on; John sent his disciples out of the starting gate that they might run toward a Christ not yet revealed, and so, lest these men flatter themselves and refuse to advance, Paul shows them they are still far from the mark — for the feeling of want is what makes a man desire what he lacks. Calvin's conclusion is the boldest in the group: John's baptism was a token of repentance and remission of sins, and our baptism today does not differ from it in anything, save that Christ is now revealed and our salvation made perfect in his death and resurrection. Wesley closes the section with a valediction: after this, John is mentioned no more, and here he gives way to Christ altogether.
37:
The recorder's next sentence is a legal acquittal, and it needs a word of translation first. Barnes calls the older English unhappy, since churches now means buildings for Christian worship and the Greek means those who plunder temples of their sacred things; Ellicott simply corrects it to robbers of temples, noting that Elizabethan writers used the word freely of heathen shrines. Robertson adds that the offence was a serious one in the ancient world — the temples often held vast treasures, like banks, and men felt about temple-robbing much as a later age felt about horse-thieves — and Ellicott reports that the corresponding noun for sacrilege turns up in inscriptions found among the ruins of the Ephesian temple itself, naming a crime to which the severest penalties were attached.

What is being certified is therefore precise. Gaius and Aristarchus had committed no act against the temple and spoken no word against the goddess. Barnes draws out what that means about the whole two years' work: Paul and his companions had preached against idols and idol worship without offering violence to any temple or stripping it of anything used in its service, and without ever, so far as any evidence goes, using harsh or reproachful language about Diana. Ellicott says the same and adds the contrast that makes it sting — they persuaded, but they did not ridicule or revile, which is probably more than could be said for Alexander and the men who put him forward. Robertson puts it as a matter of conduct rather than doctrine: these men had so borne themselves that no charge could be laid against them in either act or word, and the mob had done a rash thing in seizing men who were innocent.

Two witnesses draw the practical lesson. Barnes says men should employ reason, and not harsh or reproachful language, against any prevailing evil, since the way to remove it is to enlighten the minds of men and convince them of their error; nothing is gained by bitter and reviling words, and it is a great thing to have obtained, as Paul did, the testimony of the chief magistrate of Ephesus that no such words were ever used. Clarke agrees that this was the apostles' method — to enlighten the multitude, so that the absurdity of their errors should become apparent to them.

Calvin accepts the acquittal and refuses the definition that accompanies it. The recorder truly and rightly denies that these men are temple-robbers, but he then quietly defines sacrilege as speaking blasphemy against Diana, and that is false; for since all superstition is itself profane, the truly sacrilegious are those who transfer to idols the honour due to God alone. What is being praised in this speech, Calvin insists, is a carnal wisdom and not godliness — the man is saving the peace, not defending the truth.
38:
Having cleared the accused, the recorder tells the accusers where to go. Barnes and Clarke both explain the first phrase as a reference to court days — days appointed for judicial hearings — and Clarke thinks the words may even mean that the judges were sitting at that moment. Ellicott gives the literal sense, that the forum days are going on, and allows both readings: either the proconsul was actually in session, or it is a colloquial way of saying that court days are at hand. Robertson notes that regular court days existed whether or not one was in session just then, and that the recorder names Demetrius and the craftsmen by name as the parties responsible for the riot — a pointed thing to do in front of the crowd they had raised.

The plural deputies is a small puzzle that has produced four answers. Asia was a senatorial province governed by a proconsul, but by only one at a time. Robertson calls the plural rhetorical, a general way of naming the office. Wesley reads it as simply meaning that there is one in every province and one here. Calvin explains it from practice, that legates sometimes held court in the proconsul's place. Ellicott offers the most circumstantial solution: Junius Silanus, who was proconsul when Paul reached Ephesus, had been poisoned by the two procurators Celer and Helius at Agrippina's instigation, and it seems probable that for a time those two held a joint proconsular authority — in which case the plural is exact.

The last clause is technical, and Ellicott takes it as such. The English implead renders the Greek closely: Demetrius and his followers were to lodge a formal statement of charge, the accused to put in a rejoinder, and with issue thus joined each side would bring its witnesses. Robertson notes that Luke uses this verb six times in Acts, always of judicial proceedings, and that Page found an Ephesian inscription of Trajan's age containing several of the very words in this speech — the recorder's own title among them.

Calvin and Robertson both read the appeal as more than a procedural point. Calvin's summary of it is that private matters belong before the judgment-seat and public matters in an assembly summoned by the magistrates, not in a concourse that has run together at the instigation and caprice of one man. Robertson makes the modern application plainly: it is a definite appeal for orderly legal procedure against mob violence, in a case where money and religious prejudice had combined — and a striking rebuke to lynch-law in lands where Christianity is supposed to prevail.
39:
A second alternative is offered for anything the courts cannot handle. Barnes distinguishes the two cases: the first clause covered a private wrong done to Demetrius in his business, this one covers anything touching public affairs, the worship of Diana included. Clarke puts it more bluntly — such a matter is not the business of a mob, and must be heard in an assembly legally constituted and properly authorised to determine it. Ellicott sharpens the distinction into modern terms: if the grievance called for legislative rather than judicial action, it would have to go to the regular meeting of the citizen assembly, where the aggrieved could present their case and petition for redress.

The phrase for that body is the point of the verse, and it closes a thread Luke opened a few sentences earlier. Barnes notes that the word is the one usually rendered church, and that it is properly translated assembly here — not a tumultuous gathering but one convened in the legal manner. He adds the derivation, since it bears on the other use: the word means literally that which is called out, and the church is made up of those called out from the world. Robertson stresses the adjective rather than the noun. The settlement will come in the lawful assembly, and not in a riot like this one; and he quotes an Ephesian inscription that uses the identical phrase, prescribing something to be done at every lawful assembly. Ellicott cites the same class of evidence — an inscription directing that an image of Athena be set above the bench where the boys sat, at every regular meeting — so that the recorder is speaking the ordinary official language of his own city.

Robertson adds the constitutional fact that gives the offer its weight, and its limit. Only the Roman authorities could sanction the summoning of such an assembly. The recorder is therefore not merely recommending patience; he is telling a crowd that has convened itself illegally that the legal machinery exists, that it will hear them, and that it is not theirs to convene. Wesley describes the body in the same terms, as a regular assembly having authority to judge of religious and political affairs.

Gill's contribution is a small one and easy to pass over: the other matters are anything beyond what belongs to the craft and business of Demetrius and the artificers. That is the whole of the recorder's method in one phrase. He has taken a grievance that presented itself as a religious emergency and sorted it into two ordinary categories — a trade dispute and a public question — with a proper venue for each, and neither of them the theatre.
40:
The last argument is the one that actually works, and it is addressed to the crowd's own safety. Gill notes that they were liable to be called to account by the proconsul, or beyond him by the emperor or the senate, since the day's work could well be construed as riot and sedition. Barnes and Clarke both quote the Roman law behind that: he who raises a mob, let him be punished with death. Clarke thinks such a law probably was in force at Ephesus, precisely because the recorder appeals to it — in which case Demetrius stood in great personal danger, his life at the mercy of the men he had accused and against whom nothing disorderly could be proved.

Ellicott catches the pronoun, and it is the diplomatic stroke of the speech. The recorder says we, including himself with the rioters rather than standing over them, and reminds them of a risk they had not considered — that they might find themselves defendants rather than plaintiffs in the suit. He notes too that the verb is the same one rendered implead a moment earlier, so the threat is exact: the machinery just recommended to them could be turned the other way. And he doubts that any excuse would serve. A riotous concourse taking the law into its own hands was not something the proconsuls were disposed to overlook, and it would hardly be thought a legitimate defence that the crowd had laid hold of two Jews and wanted to lynch them.

Robertson takes the peril as entirely real and supplies the witness for it: Seneca says there was nothing on which the Romans looked with such jealousy as a tumultuous meeting. He notes the genitive absolute — there being no cause for it — and the word chosen for the gathering, a late term used both of a conspiracy and of a disorderly riot. Ellicott makes the same observation about the vocabulary and reads contempt in it: the recorder has selected the most dismissive word available, calling the whole business a mob-meeting to its face. Wesley, oddly, hears the opposite, that he wisely calls it by an inoffensive name — and both may be right, since the word is contemptuous but not legally incriminating, which is exactly what a man in his position would want.

Ellicott closes with a point about the record rather than the speech. An inscription of Trajan's date, from an aqueduct at Ephesus, contains nearly all the technical terms this speech uses — the city as temple-warden, the proconsul, the recorder, the people — set out in the same official order; and that, so far as it goes, confirms the accuracy of Luke's report of a scene he did not himself witness.
41:
The chapter ends on a formality, and the formality is the point. Robertson explains what the dismissal accomplished: by pronouncing the crowd dissolved, the recorder gave a semblance of law and order to what had been a mob, and so far protected the citizens against the very charge he had just warned them of. Gill notes only that this followed the oration and its arguments; the speech worked, and nothing else in the chapter had.

Robertson then turns to the quality of Luke's account, and his judgement is worth having. The picture is vivid and graphic and carries every mark of historical accuracy; Paul does not describe the episode in his letters and was not in the theatre at all; but Luke plainly had his details from someone who was. Aristarchus, who was afterwards with Luke at Caesarea and at Rome, is the obvious candidate — he and Gaius being lively witnesses of events in which their own lives were at stake.

The word for what was dismissed catches every commentator's eye one last time. Barnes and Clarke both note that it is the word usually rendered church, applied here to a riotous and tumultuous assemblage; Clarke calls it another proof that the term means an assembly of any kind, good or bad, legal or illegal. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem had already built a point of catechesis on exactly this verse. Since the word is applied to different things — as it is written of the multitude in the theatre of the Ephesians, that when he had thus spoken he dismissed the assembly — and since one might properly speak of a church of evil-doers, meaning the meetings of the heretics, the creed for that reason hands the learner the article and in one holy catholic Church. His practical counsel follows from it: if you are travelling in a strange city, do not ask simply where the Lord's house is, nor merely where the Church is, but where the catholic Church is.

Clarke ends with reflections that gather the whole chapter. How forcible are right words — and how much influence one prudent and sensible man may have over an unbridled multitude; what a blessing to a community the civil law is, since without it the crowd would destroy others and at last itself. He notes how brief the sunshine was, Paul's ministry having been greatly blessed here and opposed almost at once, since peace with the world cannot last long. And he names the motive that ran through the whole episode: how few would make an outward profession of religion if there were no gain connected with it. Demetrius would have made no stir for his worship had the preaching not discredited the thing by which he got his wealth; and most of the outcries raised against reformation since, Clarke says, have come from the same quarter, the cry that the Church is in danger being echoed loudest by those whose secular interest was at stake.
5:
One short sentence has carried more controversy than anything else in the chapter. Gill takes the hearers of the first clause to be the people John preached to, hearing that the Messiah had come and that Jesus was he. Barnes states the problem squarely: there is no other instance in the New Testament of anyone being baptized twice, and some critics have therefore read the verse as Luke's own account of what happened under John's ministry — that John told them to believe on Christ Jesus and then baptized them in his name.

Barnes rejects that reading on four grounds. It is not the obvious sense, and would occur to nobody without a theory to defend. John did not in fact baptize in the name of Christ Jesus; his was the baptism of repentance, and there is no evidence he ever used the name of Jesus in the form. If the verse reported John's act it would be a bare repetition of what has just been said, a tautology the sacred writers would not be guilty of. And the men on whom Paul laid his hands in the next verse are plainly those baptized here, the narrative running continuously as one transaction. Barnes' conclusion follows: John's baptism was not strictly Christian baptism. His guard against the inference men will want to draw is just as firm — there is no command to repeat Christian baptism and no example of it; these disciples were baptized now not because baptism is a thing to be done twice, but because they had never in fact been baptized as the Lord Jesus prescribed.

Clarke takes the same view and turns the guard into a warning. To be a Christian a man must be baptized in the Christian faith; these men had not been, felt it, and were baptized at once. But let one instance be produced, he demands, of anyone rebaptized who had before been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, or even in the name of Jesus alone. To iterate baptism where it has already been essentially performed he calls an awful thing, contrary to the canon law, to the best divines, to the practice of the purest ages, and to the New Testament itself. Robertson makes the point in a different key: Apollos was not rebaptized, the twelve apostles were not rebaptized, and Jesus received no baptism but John's. What was wrong here was ignorance so complete — of repentance, of the Messiahship of Jesus, of the Holy Spirit — that Paul had these men baptized not so much again as really baptized this time, on the authority of the Lord Jesus.

Calvin dissents from the whole frame of the question, and his is the minority reading in this chapter. He holds that the men of old wrongly supposed John's baptism and Christ's to be two different things, the one being a pledge of the same adoption and the same newness of life as ours — which is why we never read that Christ baptized afresh those who came to him from John. His conclusion here is that the water was not repeated at all. Luke's words import only that these men were baptized with the Spirit — it being no new thing for the name of baptism to be transferred to the gifts of the Spirit, as when the promise of the Spirit to the apostles is called a baptism (Acts 1:5; Acts 11:16) — and the clause about the laying on of hands that follows is added by way of interpretation, in the scriptural manner of stating a thing briefly and then setting it out plainly. Wesley is content that they were baptized twice, but not with the same baptism, and adds a detail nobody else troubles with: it was done by some other hand, Paul only laying his hands on them.
6:
The gesture comes first, and the grammatical-historical witnesses fix it in a series. Robertson notes that this laying on of hands is what Peter and John did in Samaria, and what was done for Paul himself at Damascus, and that in each case it was followed by the descent of the Spirit in supernatural power. Ellicott treats it as the outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace, pointing to the Samaritan precedent for the same sequence (Acts 8:14-18). Gill draws the parallel to the same end: as Peter and John laid hands on the believing Samaritans who had already been baptized by Philip, so here, and the same extraordinary effects followed.

What followed is described by two verbs, and the witnesses differ on the first. Clarke takes it plainly: they received the miraculous gift of different languages, and in those languages taught the people the great doctrines of the Christian religion — which is what he understands prophesying to mean here. Ellicott is not satisfied with that. He first corrects the tense — better they were speaking with tongues and prophesying, the verbs implying continuous action rather than a single episode — and then argues that a mere power of speaking foreign languages without learning them seems a much less adequate result of a new gift than the new enthusiasm and intensity of spiritual joy of which the tongues were the natural expression. His evidence is a matter of dating: the discussion of these two gifts in Paul's first letter to Corinth, where the connection of tongues with jubilant and ecstatic praise is unmistakable, was written not long after this incident, while the facts must still have been fresh in his memory (1 Corinthians 14:14-16).

Robertson reads both verbs as inchoative imperfects — they began to speak, they began to prophesy — and takes the whole as external and indubitable proof that the Spirit had come on twelve uninformed men now fully won to the service of Jesus as Messiah. He then adds the caution that keeps the sequence from becoming a mechanism: the baptism in water did not convey the Spirit, nor forgiveness of sins, and Paul was not a sacramentalist.

Henry, looking back at the whole exchange from its end, marks the suddenness of it. Men who a few minutes earlier had not so much as heard that there was any Holy Ghost are now themselves filled with him, for the Spirit, like the wind, blows where and when he pleases. He also passes on a suggestion about what the gifts were for: that they qualified these men for the work of the ministry, the spirit of prophecy that they might understand the mysteries of the kingdom themselves, and the gift of tongues that they might preach them to every language.
7:
Luke counts them, and the count is nearly exact. Gill observes that the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions drop the qualifying word altogether and affirm flatly that the men were twelve; and since the number was so small, he thinks the historian might well have been certain of it. Ellicott adjusts the English word order to the same end — better the men were in all about twelve — so that the phrase counts the whole group rather than hedging the figure.

What that group was is Ellicott's more interesting suggestion. The narrative as a whole seems to him to imply that these were not individual cases turning up here and there over time, but men living together as a kind of ascetic community, attending the meetings of the church and yet not sharing the fulness of its life. That would account for their being found at once and dealt with together, and for the uniformity of their answers.

Gill looks forward instead of back. These men seem to him the first materials of a gospel church at Ephesus which afterwards became very large and flourishing, and he thinks it very likely that they were among its elders. Henry reports the same conjecture, that the twelve were the elders to whom Paul committed the care and government of that church. It is worth noticing what the number is, and how little is made of it: twelve men, at the founding of a church in the greatest city of Asia, who a moment ago could not say whether the Holy Ghost had been given.
8:
Paul's practice does not change with the city. Gill notes that he had met the twelve in what seems to have been a private house, and that he now went with them to the synagogue on the sabbath, as his custom was, out of an affectionate concern for his own countrymen. Clarke states it as a rule with no exception: in every place Paul made his first offer of salvation to the Jews, and only when they rejected it did he turn to the Gentiles. eastern-antiochene John Chrysostom sees a further motive in the pattern — Paul wished the break to come from their side rather than his, so that the beginning of ceasing to assemble with them should be given by the Jews themselves; and behind that, he was provoking them to jealousy, since the Gentiles received him readily and the Jews, seeing the Gentiles receive him, repented.

What he preached is given in one phrase, and Henry and Calvin both open it out. Henry takes the kingdom of God to cover God's dominion over men and men's happiness in God — the obligations set up at creation, forfeited by sin, and renewed by the Redeemer — or, more particularly, the kingdom of the Messiah, which the Jews were expecting and about which Paul opened the scriptures and corrected their mistakes. Calvin gives the same term its prophetic weight, as the restoring promised to the fathers and to be fulfilled at the Messiah's coming, and then says what the kingdom consists in: first the free forgiveness of sins, by which God reconciles us to himself and adopts us as his people, and second newness of life, by which he fashions us after his own image. Robertson puts Paul's own understanding of it more sharply still, as the church of God which Jesus purchased with his own blood (Acts 20:28).

The two participles describe a method, and Henry takes them one at a time. Paul preached argumentatively — he disputed, giving scriptural reasons and answering objections, and the word suggests dialogue, questions put and answers received on both sides. He preached affectionately — he persuaded, using not only arguments to reach the understanding but motives to reach the affections, showing that the things he spoke of concerned his hearers themselves. And he preached undauntedly, speaking boldly as a man with no doubt about what he said, no distrust of the one who sent him, and no dread of those he said it to. Calvin's version of the same pair is compressed into a rule: Paul proved with sound reasons what he alleged, and then used the pricks of godly exhortation — for no profound disputation will make us obedient to God unless we are also moved by godly admonition. Clarke reads the first verb as holding conversations with them, and Barnes and Robertson both take the second as conative, an endeavouring rather than an achieving.

Chrysostom will not let the boldness be mistaken for aggression. You must not suppose, because you hear of his speaking boldly, that there was any harshness in it: it was of good things that he discoursed, of a kingdom — who would not have heard him? Robertson notes how unusual the run was: nowhere else, unless at Corinth, had Paul been able to speak so long in a synagogue without interruption. Ellicott pauses over what three months of it actually cost, and the arithmetic is his own contribution. The daily labour as a tentmaker went on as before, probably still in partnership with Aquila and Priscilla; the sabbaths saw him in the synagogue evening and morning, preaching that Jesus was the Christ and setting out the nature of his work and the laws of his kingdom. Henry adds only that three months was a competent time allowed them to consider of it.
9:
Three months of patient hearing end, and the turn is described as a process rather than an event. Ellicott corrects the tense to bring that out — better when some were growing hardened and disobedient — and Robertson agrees, reading both verbs as imperfects that show first a refusal to believe and afterwards a refusal to obey. Gill states the double effect as a law of the word itself: it is a savour of life unto life to some and of death unto death to others, as one sun melts the wax and hardens the clay.

What the hardened did next moved the quarrel out of doors. Barnes explains that the way spoken evil of is the gospel, the path by which God saves men; Wesley glosses it as the Christian way of worshipping God. Ellicott sees the familiar tactic: the unbelieving Jews acted at Ephesus as they had at Thessalonica, stirring suspicion among the Gentiles, and particularly among the lower sort, who were always ready for a tumult.

Paul's response is described with a verb the witnesses handle carefully. Robertson notes that he made a standing-off, a cleavage, as he had done at Corinth, and that the second verb is the old word for marking a limit or a horizon — the Jews would have called such a withdrawal apostasy, but what Paul was doing was constituting a separate church. Barnes turns it to a rule of prudence: removing believers from the society of those who would draw them away is often the best way to prevent an evil influence. Calvin makes it a rule of patience exhausted. When we have proof of desperate and incurable stubbornness we must lose our labour no longer, as Paul himself directs that a heretic be avoided after one or two admonitions (Titus 3:10); and the weak must be provided for, lest sound doctrine be subverted for them by slander. His image is blunt: Paul separated the disciples lest the goats should with their stink infect the flock of sheep, and so that the pure worshippers of God might profess freely.

Who Tyrannus was nobody can say. Barnes supposes him a Jew engaged in teaching who may not have been unfavourable to Christians, and reminds the reader that Christians then had no buildings of their own. Clarke thinks him a Jewish schoolmaster who lent his room, and dismisses as a most unlikely conjecture the idea that the word is a title and that some prince is meant. Calvin also rejects the notion of a ruler and supposes the school was built at the charge of a man of that name and given to the city, so that the believers were using a public place bearing its founder's name. Ellicott and Robertson both trace the name to an inscription in the columbarium of the Empress Livia's household, where it belongs to a court physician; since names and callings in that class were commonly hereditary, they raise the possibility of a physician of the same family lecturing at Ephesus, who might have known Luke. Ellicott adds the shrewdest argument for it: an unconverted teacher of rhetoric was not likely to lend his class-room to a preacher of the new faith.

Barnes objects to the translation of the last participle, calling disputing an unhappy rendering, since the word need not denote contention and is often used of reasoning or of public preaching; Wesley simply says discoursing, and notes that it now happened daily and not on the sabbath only. Robertson passes on a detail from the Codex Bezae, which specifies the hours Paul had the hall — from the fifth to the tenth, that is from just before midday until two hours before sunset. Calvin draws the moral: this place shows how continual Paul's diligence was, and how churlish are those who grow weary of learning at once.
10:
The two years are counted from the end of the three months, as Gill notes, and Robertson raises the difficulty that comes with them. Paul afterwards told the Ephesian elders that he had laboured among them for three years (Acts 20:31), which Robertson takes as a general expression covering the months in the synagogue, the two years in the hall, and a further period afterwards — perhaps in the house of Aquila and Priscilla, the season Luke mentions further on.

How a man who stayed in one city could be said to have reached a whole province is the real question of the verse, and the witnesses answer it three ways. Clarke thinks Paul did not confine himself to the lecture-room at all, and asks bluntly how otherwise all Asia could have heard: he supposes journeys through the towns and villages. Ellicott makes Ephesus the centre of activity from which such journeys radiated, and draws a conclusion that reaches beyond the chapter — we may legitimately think of the other six churches addressed in the Revelation as owing their origin to this period. Calvin denies the premise that anybody had to travel. Luke does not mean that the men of Asia came to hear Paul, but that the savour of his preaching went through all Asia and the seed was sown far and wide; it often happens that when the truth is preached in one place it sounds where the minister's own voice cannot reach, being delivered from hand to hand, one man teaching another. His comment on why that is necessary is the sharpest sentence in the group: one man would not be sufficient, unless every man were diligent for himself to spread the faith abroad.

Robertson supplies what the record elsewhere shows about those helpers and those years, and it is a crowded picture. The gospel reached the Lycus valley and the rest of the seven churches; Paul had men like Epaphras and Philemon carrying the message over the province, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia were with him later. Meanwhile these were the years of his greatest anxiety over Corinth — a letter now lost, messages from the household of Chloe, a letter from the church, Timothy sent and then Titus, and the writing of the first epistle we possess — all of it while the work at Ephesus went on. He adds a witness from outside scripture: forty years afterwards Pliny wrote to Trajan from Bithynia that the contagion of this superstition had spread not only through cities but through villages and country places.

Two of the witnesses mark what the phrase both Jews and Greeks covers. Clarke takes the Greeks to mean not merely the proselytes of the gate but the heathen at large, and notes that although Paul had ceased preaching in the synagogue the Jews continued to hear him in the school. Barnes explains the constant influx into Ephesus for commerce and worship that made such a hearing possible. Wesley marks the timing rather than the extent: Paul had once been forbidden to preach the word in Asia (Acts 16:6), and now the time was come. Ellicott adds the detail that will matter shortly — the growth of the new community had begun to tell on the number of pilgrims bringing offerings to the shrine of Artemis and carrying memorials away.
11:
Luke's adjective is not the one a reader expects, and every witness stops on it. Ellicott points out that the Greek phrase is negative rather than positive: no common works of power, not such as one might meet with any day. Robertson calls it litotes for the extraordinary and notes the construction is peculiar to Luke in the New Testament, though it occurs in classical writers, in the third book of Maccabees, and in the papyri and inscriptions. Barnes finds the same expression in Longinus, who says of Moses that he was no common man. Clarke renders it miracles of no ordinary kind.

Ellicott adds an observation about the noun that quietly identifies the narrator. The word for these powers is the one physicians used technically for the healing virtues of this or that remedy, and its free use here is so far characteristic of Luke — a small mark of the same professional habit of mind that will make him linger over the details of the next verse.

Gill draws the distinction the phrase forces: these were not common and vulgar miracles, and still less were they things of chance or accident, but rare and uncommon works in which there was a visible display of the power of God — who is the efficient cause, the apostle being only an instrument he made use of. Calvin puts the same point on the idiom of the sentence. It is a common manner of speech that wonders and signs are wrought by the hand of men, so that the praise is ascribed to God alone as the author and the man is only the minister; and the purpose was that Paul's apostleship should be set forth with these ensigns, so that his doctrine might carry the greater authority. Wesley says it in five words, that they were wrought in a very uncommon manner. Robertson notes the imperfect tense — God kept on working them — and gives the reason such unusual proofs were called for here. In Samaria, Philip's miracles had been needed to break the hold of Simon Magus; at Ephesus, exorcists and magicians had built an enormous vogue of false spiritualism, and Paul was facing unseen forces of evil.

Robertson also names the danger in the success, and it is the thread the rest of the section follows: this extraordinary power led some people into superstitious practices, on the assumption that there was something potent in Paul's own person.
12:
Two Latin words in a Greek sentence tell the reader what kind of cloth is meant. Barnes and Ellicott both identify them: the first is the linen used to wipe sweat from the brow or face, the word that elsewhere names the napkin in a parable and the cloth bound about the face of Lazarus; the second is the short apron worn round the waist by artisans at their work. Gill fills in the domestic sense of both — what Paul might use to wipe his face, and what he would wear as a mechanic while working at his trade — and notes that the Ethiopic and Syriac versions render the phrase as being of the garments upon his body.

Ellicott asks the question the passage really raises: why should Luke, who has just passed over two years in a single sentence, dwell so particularly on handkerchiefs and aprons? His first answer is the physician's habit of mind, which would lead him to dwell on the phenomena of a supernatural gift of healing; his second is his conjecture about Tyrannus, a report likely enough to pass from one physician to another. The picture he draws is domestic and precise — devout people coming to the apostle as he worked at his craft and carrying away the very cloths he had used.

What that efficacy amounts to divides the witnesses sharply. Barnes denies any virtue in the objects at all: there was no more power in the aprons than in the hem of the garment the woman touched, or in the clay used to open the blind man's eyes; the cloths were a sign only, evidence to all concerned that the healing came by Paul's instrumentality, just as the Saviour putting his fingers into a deaf man's ears was evidence to onlookers of where the power lay (Mark 7:33). Ellicott is readier to allow the medium a real function, though not a power of its own: the two conditions of a healing work are divine power on one side and faith on the other, and any external medium may serve to strengthen the second and bring it into contact with the first — on which footing, he says, cures ascribed to relics admit in some measure of a like explanation. Calvin had already ruled that inference out in the strongest terms available to him, insisting that Paul chose the most worthless things he had precisely so that no superstition should arise from their price or their pomp, and that to wrest this passage into a defence of relics is to make the apostle send out his handkerchiefs to be kissed. Robertson answers from the other end. There is no power in superstition or in magic, but there is power in God; and if God never honoured any faith except such as was entirely free from superstition, one might ask about Christians who are troubled over a number or a moon or a rabbit's foot. God condescends to meet us in our ignorance, at the point where he can reach us — as he met the woman who touched the hem, and those who sought the shadow of Peter (Acts 5:15), and Elisha, who supposed that something of Elijah's power resided in his mantle (2 Kings 2:13).

The last clause holds a distinction Clarke will not let pass. The diseases departed and the evil spirits went out: a most evident difference is made between the two, so that they were not one and the same thing. Wesley qualifies it from the other side, allowing that the evil spirits also occasioned many diseases that might yet appear purely natural. Ellicott closes with what the episode taught the city: it was something for such a population to learn that a prayer of faith and a workman's apron had more power to heal than the charms they had trusted.
13:
The trade is described before the men are named. Gill has them strolling from place to place, pretending to tell fortunes, cure diseases by charms and dispossess devils by conjuration. Barnes rescues the word the older English calls them by — it means only one wandering from place to place, without any settled habitation, and not what a vagabond has come to mean since — and explains the technical title: exorcists were so called from a verb meaning to bind with an oath, because in their operations they adjured the spirits, commonly by the name of God. Robertson compares them to modern fortune-tellers going the rounds, and notes that spells connected with Solomon's name were a Jewish speciality, attested by Josephus and alluded to by Jesus himself when he asked by whom the children of his accusers cast them out (Matthew 12:27).

Why they should reach for this particular name is the point of the story, and the witnesses agree on the motive. Clarke says it plainly: finding that Paul cast out demons by the name of Jesus, they supposed that by using it themselves they might produce the same effects, which would be an ample source of revenue in a place where demoniacs abounded. Barnes gives the two reasons that would have occurred to them — that Jesus had expelled many evil spirits, and that it was in his name that Paul wrought his miracles — and suspects they took the name for a charm. Ellicott is sharpest on what that means: to men of this class the name of the Lord Jesus was simply one more formula, mightier perhaps than the name of the Most High God or of the archangels which others used. Robertson notices the article in their sentence, as though they were identifying the right magic word to the demons, and adds the assumption underneath it — that success turned on getting the formula exactly right, the Ephesian mysteries having room, as they supposed, for Christianity too. Chrysostom sees the same thing in the wording and says it in one line: so entirely did they do everything by way of trade — they had no mind to believe, but by that Name they wished to cast out the demons.

Henry works out what such men could have hoped to gain either way, and the calculation is worth following. If the spirits yielded to an adjuration in the name of Jesus made by men who did not believe in him, they could say that the name proved nothing about his doctrine; if the spirits did not yield, they could say his name was less powerful than the others they used. Their own formula gives them away — not whom we believe in or depend upon, but whom Paul preacheth, as if to say, we will try what that name will do.

Calvin traces the office itself to a bad root. God had in times past used the prophets to drive away devils, and under colour of that men invented conjuration and erected an extraordinary function without any commandment of God. He then presses the charge into his own century, against a church that ordains exorcists as a step on the way to higher orders and then never puts the office into practice. The invocation here, he says, had two faults at once: strangers to Paul's doctrine, they used the colour of it without faith, as a magical enchantment; and they took to themselves, uncalled, what is not in any man's hand. Wesley says the same thing with a shorter fuse — a vain undertaking, for Satan laughs at all who attempt to expel him except by faith, and all the light of reason is nothing against the craft of that subtle spirit.
14:
The description of the father is the difficulty, and no two witnesses settle it the same way. Barnes rules out the obvious sense at once: this cannot mean the high priest of the Jews, since it is wholly improbable that his sons would be wandering exorcists; it must mean that he was of the priestly order, a priest of distinction who had held office as a ruler. Ellicott allows that the phrase might mean the head of one of the twenty-four courses into which the temple priesthood was divided, but thinks it hardly probable that a man in that position would take up so disreputable a calling — and offers the neatest solution in the group: the title itself was part of the imposture. He called himself a chief priest, and Luke, or the informant behind Luke, described him as he described himself.

Clarke reaches a similar result by a different road, preferring the reading of the Codex Bezae, which makes him simply a certain priest and gives the whole encounter in a fuller form. He then supplies the background against which the whole trade should be read, quoting at length Josephus' account of Eleazar, who released demoniacs in the presence of Vespasian and his officers by holding a ring with a certain root under the man's nostrils, and who proved his power by setting a cup of water at a distance and commanding the departing demon to overturn it. Clarke's own verdict is unsparing: the ring, the root, the cup and the spell all indicate imposture, and it is a further question altogether whether such arts, even if they came from Solomon, were any part of the wisdom he received from God. He adds the Jewish name for such practitioners — masters of the Name — who claimed that a right pronunciation of the sacred name could work wonders, and who fell back on that explanation when they could not deny the miracles of Christ.

Robertson admits ignorance and asks the questions the verse leaves open. Who Sceva was we do not know; some manuscripts read ruler rather than priest, and the name may be Latin in origin. What the number tells him is a judgement on the city: that a man of priestly family should have seven sons in so degraded a business shows how poorly Judaism had fared in this superstitious place. He wonders too whether the seven imagined some special power in their number, and Ellicott suspects the same, picturing them standing in a body before a demoniac as frenzied and as strong as the Gadarene.

Henry's response is grief rather than analysis. It is sad to see the house of Jacob so degenerated, and sadder to see the house of Aaron, the family peculiarly consecrated to God, in league with Satan. The temple would have found employment and encouragement enough for the sons of a chief priest, had there been twice as many; it was a vain and rambling humour, he supposes, that led them to turn mountebanks instead and wander the world over.
15:
The answer comes from the wrong side of the room, and its two verbs are not the same verb. Clarke marks the change and renders it accordingly — I acknowledge Jesus, and am acquainted with Paul; but of whom are ye? — and cites an old English Bible that kept the distinction. Ellicott gives the difference its weight: the first implies a recognition of authority, the second a more familiar acquaintance. Robertson makes the same separation and adds that the closing question is emphatic by its very word order — but you, who are you?

Barnes puts the sense in terms of jurisdiction. The power of Jesus to cast out devils the spirit knows; the power given to Paul it knows; what it denies is that these men have any standing at all — they belong to neither party, and have no right to attempt anything in either name. Ellicott adds the psychology of the moment, noting that the possessed man identifies himself with the demon as the Gadarene did, and stood in awe of the Name when it was uttered by a man like Paul, but saw no reason to fear seven pretenders who had borrowed it.

Henry hears in the reply something more than a demon's contempt. It was extorted out of the mouth of the evil spirit by the power of God, to gain honour for the gospel and to shame those who made a bad use of Christ's name; and he supplies the words the spirit might have added out of the psalm — what have you to do to declare the power of Jesus, or to take his covenant into your mouths, seeing you hate his instructions (Psalms 50:16-17)? Henry then turns the sentence outward, against every power and faction that professes a mighty zeal for Jesus and Paul while serving a merely worldly interest: Jesus we know, and Paul we know, but who are you?

Gill notes only that several of the versions add the words to them, fixing the address on the seven — which is the whole point of the retort. The spirit does not dispute the name. It disputes the men.
16:
What follows is described with a violence the Greek makes vivid. Robertson takes the first verb as an ingressive aorist of a word used of a panther springing on its prey, and the second as an effective aorist meaning to become master of; the word rendered both, he notes from the papyri, can cover more than two and here takes in all seven. Barnes and Ellicott both refer the strength to the possession itself, Ellicott comparing the preternatural strength of frenzy in the Gadarene (Mark 5:3-4) and observing that men of the impostors' class are commonly more or less cowards, so that they fled in dismay before the man's paroxysms. Clarke draws the inference as a question: one man proved stronger than seven brothers, stripped them and wounded them all — was this not proof enough where his strength came from?

The two words describing their retreat need less than they seem to. Ellicott points out that the first need not imply more than that the outer cloak was torn away, leaving them in the short tunic; Robertson says the same, taking it of torn garments, and notes that the participle behind wounded is a perfect passive of a verb Luke uses only once elsewhere.

Ellicott then makes an observation about the shape of the narrative that is worth more than any of the philology. It may be noted, as an indication of truthfulness, that the story stops here. A writer inventing miracles would surely have crowned it by having the man who baffled the impostors healed at once by the apostle's power; Luke leaves him unhealed and says nothing further about him.

Calvin is careful about the grammar of possession. What the devil did is attributed to the man, since a man could not of himself have put seven strong young men to flight; and Luke is speaking here of a particular kind of indwelling, where Satan has the bridle so far that he possesses the whole man. God's purpose in permitting the scene, Calvin adds, was to show that his power is not contained in the sound of a voice, and that it is not lawful to abuse the name of his Son superstitiously. Henry draws the warning for the other side of the door: this is written for all who name the name of Christ without departing from iniquity. Resist the devil by a true and lively faith and he will flee; think to resist him by the bare use of Christ's name, as a spell or a charm, and he will prevail.
17:
What happened in a private house did not stay there. Gill supposes there were spectators enough, Jews and Greeks both, to carry the story through the city; Calvin takes the phrase known to all in the ordinary sense of commonly or everywhere, and sees a purpose in the publicity — the matter was much talked of among the people, so that the name of Christ might be made known to more men than had heard it before. Robertson calls the outcome a notable victory over the powers of evil in Ephesus, and notes that the verb is an imperfect: the name went on being magnified.

Two effects are recorded, and Henry separates them. Men were terrified, because in one scene they had seen at once the malice of the devil whom they served and the power of the Christ whom they opposed, and both were awful considerations; and God was glorified, since the name by which his faithful servants cast out devils without resistance now appeared to be a name above every name. Barnes puts the same conclusion evidentially: impostors could not work such miracles, and those who pretended to only exposed themselves to the rage of the spirits, so that the failure of the seven served to demonstrate a real and vital difference between them and Paul, and extended rather than damaged the reputation of the gospel.

Ellicott states the lesson the city actually drew. The sacred Name stood on quite a different level from the other names the exorcists had been employing; it was a perilous thing to use it rashly, without inward faith in all that it implied; and men thought more of it than before precisely because they had seen what fell on those who profaned it. Henry adds the negative half of that lesson, which mattered at Ephesus more than anywhere: the religion of Christ was not to be compounded with pagan superstition, and his name was not to be trifled with.

Clarke follows the practice forward instead of back. Adjurations of evil spirits were frequent in the primitive church, he says, and there the name of Jesus alone was used; exorcists came in time to form a distinct order alongside presbyters, deacons, lectors and door-keepers, and the adjuration was commonly pronounced over catechumens before their baptism — a rite of which Gregory of Nazianzen and other early writers have much to say. Wesley closes the episode with the shortest verdict of all, and it is the one the narrative bears out: even the malice of the devil here wrought for the furtherance of the gospel.
18:
The fear that fell on the city produced something more specific than awe. Robertson reads the imperfect as a stream rather than an occasion — they kept coming, one after another — and is candid about who they were: even believers had been secretly under the spell of these false spiritualists, much as some Christians now keep private contacts with so-called occult powers of which they are ashamed. What the defeat of the exorcists had done was open their eyes; judgment, he says, was beginning at the house of God, and it was time to make a clean breast of it. Gentile converts had a hard struggle to shake off the environment they came from.

Ellicott sharpens the translation to the same effect: better many of those that had believed, the word covering the whole process of conversion including baptism, so that in this instance the confession follows the rite instead of preceding it. He allows that the text does not say whether it was made privately to Paul and the other teachers or publicly before the congregation, but thinks the latter much the more probable, on the analogy of the confession made to the Baptist (Matthew 3:6). His account of the psychology is the fullest anyone gives: in some a vague awe at this contact with the unseen, in others a newly definite belief in Christ as the judge of all men, roused conscience into intense activity, so that the sins of their past lives came back on their memories and it was a relief to throw the burden off. Wesley says it more briefly — the efficacy of God's word penetrating the inmost recesses of the soul wrought a free and open confession that torments might not have compelled.

Barnes turns the verse into a test. The deeds shown are directly the magical practices, though the word may cover iniquity in general; and a man who makes a profession of religion will be willing to confess, for no one can have evidence that he is truly renewed who is not willing to confess as well as to forsake his sins — he that covereth them shall not prosper (Proverbs 28:13).

Calvin values the confession precisely because it was not required. Men count nothing more precious than their reputation, and it is a hard matter to wring a true confession out of an offender; so no man who is not thoroughly touched will make himself subject to the reproaches of others, and willingly be judged on earth that he may be acquitted in heaven. From that he refuses to build a rule. Luke does not prescribe a common law for all men here, but sets before them an example for those who need the same medicine. He then presses the distinction against the auricular confession of his own day, point by point: these men confessed how they had been deceived before they came to the faith, not every word and deed and thought; they did it once, not yearly; of their own accord, not under compulsion; many of them came, not all; and they humbled themselves before the whole company of the faithful, rather than whispering into the ear of a single priest.
19:
The phrase rendered curious arts is a technical one, and the witnesses unpack it before they touch the bonfire. Barnes takes it of things requiring skill, address and cunning, and so of magic and sleight of hand; Ellicott of superstitious arts overbusy with the supposed secrets of the invisible world; Robertson notes that the word means originally a busybody or a piddler about trifles, and that the papyri and inscriptions confirm it as the trade term for magic. Calvin widens it deliberately: the Greek covers whatever has no sound benefit in it but leads men's minds through crooked and unprofitable ways, and judicial astrology and every kind of divination about the time to come belong under it as much as conjuring does.

What the books held is well enough attested to be described. The Ephesian letters were famous in antiquity, and Clarke, Barnes and Ellicott between them assemble the evidence: slips of parchment worn on the body, inscribed with words of lost or minimal meaning, which Clement of Alexandria records and interprets as Darkness and Light, the Earth and the Year, the Sun and Truth. Clarke passes on the story from Suidas of the wrestler at the Olympic games who could not be thrown while the letters were bound to his heels, and who was thrown thirty times as soon as they were found and taken away; Barnes cites Plutarch, that magicians made the possessed recite the letters in a certain order, and Eustathius, that the Ephesians were saved thirteen times by them in their war with Miletus. Ellicott suspects the whole apparatus is a survival of the old Phrygian worship of the powers of nature, older in the city than the Greek name of Artemis. Robertson adds that Deissmann took the burned books to have been very much like the magical papyri since recovered from Egypt.

Ellicott alone tries to explain why the burning happened when it did, and his answer joins the two preceding scenes. The deep-ingrained superstition of the people had been treated homoeopathically. Charms and names had been allowed to serve as channels of renewal — the aprons in one scene — but had then been shown to have no virtue of their own, being media only between divine power on one side and faith on the other, which is what the rout of the seven exorcists demonstrated; and so the disease was cured. He notes that the tense makes the burning continuous, whether often repeated or lasting some hours, and finds a modern parallel in Florence, where artists and musicians carried their pictures and ornaments and costly dresses into the Piazza of St Mark at the bidding of Savonarola.

On the price the witnesses simply disagree. Barnes reckons the coin most probably the Attic drachm, giving a figure far below what it would be if Jewish shekels were meant; Ellicott settles on the same drachma and computes about seventeen hundred pounds, adding that in purchasing power — a drachma being a day's wage — it stood for a great deal more; Clarke works through sestertii and denarii and arrives at figures ranging from four hundred pounds to sixteen hundred; Robertson estimates roughly two thousand; Wesley, taking shekels, reaches over six thousand. Calvin declines to settle it, but insists on what the number is there to convey — that the faithful valiantly despised gain. Henry adds several other motives: they showed a holy indignation at the sins they had been guilty of, cut off any road back, removed a temptation, and prevented the books doing mischief to anyone else. Had Judas been present, he says, he would have proposed selling them and giving the money to the poor. Wesley agrees that burning was far better than selling, even for the poor's sake; and Robertson allows himself a wish that in every city the degrading books could be piled together and burned in the same way.
20:
The summary sentence is built out of two verbs and an adverbial phrase, and each has been looked at. Robertson notes that the phrase means according to strength, a common military term in Thucydides and found nowhere else in the New Testament, and that both verbs are imperfects: the word kept growing and kept gaining strength. Ellicott makes the same point about continuity and adds that the better manuscripts read the word of the Lord. Calvin takes the phrase to mark an efficacy greater than usual, and then divides the two verbs between two effects — the growing he refers to numbers, the church being increased as new disciples were gathered daily, and the prevailing to the men already gathered, who profited more and more in obedience and godliness as their faith took deeper root. Wesley compresses the same division into a clause: in extent, and in power and efficacy.

Henry works out what each half looks like from the outside. The word grows extensively when those least likely to yield, and stiffest in their opposition, are captivated and brought into obedience; it prevails when strong corruptions are mortified, vicious habits changed, evil customs of long standing broken off, and sins that were pleasant, gainful and fashionable are abandoned. Gill lists what it had prevailed over in this city, and the list is the chapter in miniature: conjuring books, conjurers themselves, and the devils behind them. He also notes a textual curiosity — one ancient copy reads the faith of God, and the Syriac faith in God — which Clarke reports too, from the Codex Bezae, where the clause about faith increasing and multiplying is added outright.

Barnes reads the whole episode as the settling of a principle, and states it as bluntly as anyone in the corpus. Religion has power to break a sinner's hold on dishonest means of living; the abandonment ought to be as public as the offence was; and the only question is what is right, not what it will cost. He then applies it without softening. A converted slave-trader's duty is not to sell his ship to a man who will continue the traffic, nor a distiller's to sell his distillery to someone who will go on making the drink; the property is to be withdrawn from the trade publicly, destroyed or turned to some useful purpose. Every excuse about loss of livelihood that is made in defence of such trades, he observes, might equally have been made by the men who owned these books — and if those excuses are good, then these men were fools, and ought to have sold their volumes to somebody who would go on using them.

Two witnesses look past the sentence to what surrounded it. Clarke thinks it was probably about this time that Paul fought with beasts at Ephesus, in whatever sense he meant that (1 Corinthians 15:32) — severe trials not recorded here, unless the reference is to the riot that closes the chapter. Robertson looks the other way, forward: this was a day of triumph in a city of vast wealth and superstition, and Ephesus would be a centre of Christian strength for centuries, drawing Timothy, and John, and Polycarp, and Irenaeus after it.
22:
The plan is put into motion by sending two men ahead. Gill supposes they went to Philippi or Thessalonica or Berea, to give notice of Paul's coming and prepare for him. Barnes thinks Timothy an obvious choice, having been in Macedonia when the churches there were founded, and is more interested in his companion: Erastus was the treasurer of the city of Corinth (Romans 16:23), and therefore exactly the right man to send on an errand that involved gathering the collection for the poor at Jerusalem — Paul having had wit enough to employ someone accustomed to handling money.

Ellicott lights the mission from Paul's own letters. Timothy was sent forward to warn and exhort, so that Paul might not have to use severity when he came himself; Paul asked the Corinthians to receive him in such a way that his youth should not detract from his authority (1 Corinthians 16:10); and he was back with Paul by the time the second letter was written. Erastus, he agrees, is the chamberlain of Corinth, chosen probably because his office would carry weight of its own. Robertson fills in what happened next, and the sequence is not tidy: Timothy did not quite succeed in placating the divided church, so Titus was despatched after him to finish the work, with instructions to meet Paul at Troas. Clarke adds the later notice that Erastus was eventually left behind at Corinth (2 Timothy 4:20).

Why Paul stayed is the question the last clause raises. Robertson renders it literally — he himself had additional time in Asia — and supplies the reason from the letter Paul was writing at just this moment: a great door was standing wide open at Ephesus, and he meant to remain until Pentecost (1 Corinthians 16:8). Here, he observes, Luke and Paul supplement each other, since Luke gives the delay and Paul the motive. Robertson also notes what the calendar meant in that city: May was the month of the festival of Artemis, when great multitudes came to Ephesus — and in the event Paul did not stay to Pentecost at all, because the uproar of Demetrius hurried him away sooner than he had planned. Clarke offers a quieter reason for the same delay, that Paul remained to gather the collection for the saints; the two are not incompatible, and the chapter is about to supply a third.
21:
A new stage of the narrative opens here, as Robertson observes: the book begins to have Rome on its horizon at this verse and ends with Paul in the city. The phrase that carries the turn is the disputed one. Barnes renders it flatly as resolved in his mind. Ellicott prefers in spirit and argues that the Greek implies more than human volition, the spirit which formed the purpose being in communion with the Divine Spirit. Calvin takes it further — Paul purposed his journey by the instinct and motion of the Spirit, so that we may know his whole life was framed to God's pleasure; and he adds the point that makes the reading bearable when the journey turns out otherwise than planned. God often governs his servants while concealing the issue from them, since he will have them follow what he has shown them even with their eyes shut in a doubtful case. Chrysostom hears the same thing in the words, that all Paul did was done not of his own power, and treats the closing sentence as prophecy — spoken partly to comfort the disciples, who would understand that he was not going away from them but coming nearer.

Henry leaves both readings open, allowing either Paul's own spirit or the direction of the Holy Spirit by whom he was led. On the itinerary he is more definite. The visit to Macedonia and Achaia was to see how the work went on and to rectify what was amiss; the visit to Jerusalem was to report to the brethren there; and the intention on Rome was not a tourist's. To see Rome was a common enough expression for looking about the famous city, but what Paul designed was to see the Christians in it and do them some service (Romans 1:11). Henry passes on Lightfoot's suggestion that the plan became possible only on the death of Claudius, since while that emperor lived the Jews were banished from Rome.

What lay behind the plan is supplied from the letters. Ellicott finds two motives joined. There was anxiety about Corinth, where a letter now lost had already been needed to warn against the city's besetting impurity, and where the people of Chloe had brought word of schisms and grave disorders in worship and discipline; and there was the intention of appearing at Jerusalem as the bearer of a munificent contribution from the Gentile churches to the suffering church of the Hebrews. Barnes thinks the collection was the main object of the journey; Clarke supposes the first letter to Corinth was written from Ephesus in this same period, to correct those very abuses. Robertson notes that the route named here is not the one Paul first intended — he had meant to reach Achaia first and Macedonia afterwards, and changed the order, perhaps because of the bad news. Chrysostom sees him in that letter excusing himself to the Corinthians for having loitered, and pointing them to the trouble that came upon him in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8).

Two witnesses close on what the sentence shows about the man. Calvin notes that he was so wholly given to the profit of the churches that he would rather deprive himself of Timothy — the most faithful and dearest and fittest of his companions — than leave the Macedonians unprovided for. Wesley looks at the whole reach of the plan: Paul sought no rest but pressed on as though he had done nothing yet; already possessed of Ephesus and Asia, he purposes Macedonia and Achaia, has his eye on Jerusalem, then on Rome, and afterwards on Spain — and no Caesar and no Alexander, Wesley says, comes up to the magnanimity of this little Benjamite. Barnes adds the quiet sentence that the rest of the book will bear out: he did go to Rome, but he went in chains.
23:
The understatement is deliberate, and Robertson names it as such — a litotes, no small stir, in a phrase Luke uses only once besides. What the stir was about is given the name that has run through the chapter already: the Way, which by now serves as a title for the whole movement. Gill notes that the versions gloss it variously as the way of God, the way of the Lord, or simply this doctrine; Barnes and Clarke both take it of the gospel Paul preached, and Ellicott simply corrects the article. Robertson adds that this was not the first trouble at Ephesus — the fight with beasts Paul mentions in a letter written before this uproar had already happened, and since a Roman citizen could not be thrown to beasts, he was picturing his violent opponents in that phrase.

Calvin sets the timing against Paul's own hopes. He had expected, when he began arranging his journey, that the church would be quiet after his departure; and instead an uproar rises suddenly in the quarter where he least feared one. From the man who raises it Calvin draws the moral he will spend the rest of his comment enlarging: covetousness is a hurtful plague, since one man for the sake of his own gain does not hesitate to trouble a whole city with sedition. The craftsmen who catch fire from him teach a second lesson — how easy it is to move men whose belly is their god to any kind of wickedness, especially men who live from day to day on the gain of a single trade, when the hope of that gain is taken away.
