Calvin then turns the scene on his own century, and the comparison is unsparing. Demetrius raised a tumult because, if the superstition by which he made his living were taken away, his craft would fall to the ground; and he did not lack an honest colour for it, pleading the worship of Diana. The clergy Calvin has in view boast that they strive for the catholic faith, but the matter itself declares that they fight not so much for the altars as for the fires — that they may have hot kitchens. They can wink at blasphemies against God so long as their revenues are untouched, and are courageous only in maintaining the superstitions that serve their purpose. From this he draws two counsels. Let a man choose a way of life that agrees with the doctrine of Christ, lest the desire of gain provoke him into an ungodly combat; and let faithful teachers expect adversaries as long as the world stands, since every affection of the flesh is an enemy to God, and there are as many armed enemies to Christ as there are lusts in the world.

Behind Demetrius, Calvin insists, stands someone else. His covetousness is manifest enough; but he was Satan's bellows, and an enemy who seeks by every means to overthrow the doctrine of Christ found in him a fit instrument. That is the frame in which the rest of the chapter should be read: what follows is a riot about silverwork, and it is also, on this reading, a campaign.
24:
Everything in the scene turns on what Demetrius actually made, and the witnesses do not agree. Barnes explains that the word rendered shrine means properly a case or small chest in which sacred things are kept, and takes these to be small portable temples of silver, made to resemble the temple of Diana and probably containing a silver image of the goddess — the sort of thing pilgrims and strangers would buy, since the temple was one of the seven wonders of the world. Clarke and Wesley agree that they were models of the building itself, Clarke suggesting they served as a substitute for the temple among worshippers in distant parts of Greece. Ellicott and Robertson both correct that: the word is the one used elsewhere for the inner sanctuary rather than the whole building, so what was reproduced was the chapel in which the statue stood, and the statue with it. Chrysostom, reading in Greek, had already put the difficulty as a question — how is it possible that temples should be made of silver? — and guessed at small boxes. Robertson adds two complications. No silver shrines have been dug up at Ephesus, only terra-cotta ones, which Ramsay explains by supposing the silver were melted down, the poorer votaries buying clay and the richer silver; and an inscription in the city names a Demetrius who was a temple-warden, which led Zoeckler to suggest that Luke had mistaken that title for silversmith.

About the temple itself the record is fuller. Clarke gives its dimensions and the hundred and twenty-seven columns raised at the charge of as many kings, and the two hundred and twenty years it took to build; Ellicott traces its history from the magnificence it owed to Croesus, through its burning by a man who wanted an immortality of infamy, to its rebuilding in Alexander's time and the paintings and sculptures of the great Greek masters in its porticos. He describes an establishment that reminds him of a mediaeval cathedral — priests, attendants and boys, schooling for the children of the temple service, pensions for those who retired at sixty, great gifts and bequests, and a class of interpreters of the mysteries who were called theologians. Robertson dates the burning to the night Alexander was born, as Clarke does; and Chrysostom preserves the measure of the city's grief at it, that they forbade the incendiary's name ever to be mentioned.

The image was another matter entirely. Ellicott insists that it bore no resemblance to the sculptured beauty in which Greek and Roman art loved to represent Artemis: a many-breasted figure ending below the breast in a square column, carved in wood, black with age, its ornament a strange mingling of bees and ears of corn and flowers, with no form or beauty at all — closer, he says, to a Hindu idol than a Greek statue, and a survival of an older worship of the powers of nature. Then he offers the observation that lifts the paragraph: its ugliness was perhaps the secret of its power, for when art clothes idolatry with beauty a man feels free to criticise the artist, and reverence grows weaker by degrees. Robertson agrees on the substance, that this Artemis was a goddess of fertility like the Lydian Cybele and quite distinct from the huntress sister of Apollo whom the Romans called Diana.

What made it a trade is the last clause, and two witnesses read it as an organisation rather than an accident. Robertson takes the imperfect middle to mean that the business kept coming in, and reads Demetrius as the leader of a guild he had probably formed and financed himself. Chrysostom states the principle the whole episode illustrates, and states it flatly: wherever there is idolatry, in every case we find money at the bottom of it.
25:
The meeting Demetrius calls is not quite what a modern reader assumes. Robertson points out that employer and employees are in the room together, so this is not a strike but a gathering of the associated trades in protest against a preacher. Ellicott distinguishes the two groups the verse names: the craftsmen of the previous sentence are the higher sort of skilled labour, artists in a real sense, while the workmen of like occupation are the artisans they employed. Gill takes the first group to be the masters of the trade, of whom Demetrius was one.

The opening sentence of his speech is the one everyone stops at. Barnes notes that the word rendered wealth means acquisition or property and does not assert that these men were rich, only that they depended on the trade for a living; Clarke says it carries the sense of abundance and calls the trade most lucrative; Robertson traces the word to a root meaning easy to pass through, and observes what Demetrius is doing with it — appealing to self-interest as the basis of zeal for Artemis, piety for the sake of revenue. Chrysostom notices the asymmetry the speech conceals: Demetrius was wealthy himself and could have borne the loss, while the men he was addressing were poor and lived on their daily earnings; and it is worth observing that they said nothing, and only he spoke.

Ellicott draws the general principle out and then turns it uncomfortably. The words of Demetrius bring before us, with an almost naive simplicity, that element of vested interest which has at all times played so large a part in resistance to reform, and which entered deeply into the persecutions the first preachers met. Every city had its temples and priests and sanctuaries; sacrifices and feasts created a market for industry that would not otherwise have existed. But the Church in its later development, employing the services of art, encouraging pilgrimages and organising its institutions, created a market of another kind and so gave rise to vested interests of its own, which in their turn became obstacles to reformation. At the outset it was the very absence of the aesthetic element in Christian life that threatened men in these trades with the loss of their livelihood, and roused them to a fierce antagonism.

Calvin will not allow the plea any dignity at all. It is lawful in some measure for a man to provide for his own profit; to trouble the public peace for gain, to overthrow equity and right, to give oneself over to violence, and to set out deliberately to extinguish what is just — that is another thing. Demetrius states the case honestly enough, that Paul denies those to be gods which are made with hands, and then never asks whether it is true; blinded by the desire of gain, he is carried headlong to oppress a true doctrine, and the same blindness drives him to violent remedies. The craftsmen, afraid of poverty and hunger, run as fast, for the belly is blind and deaf and can admit no equity. Calvin ends by turning the case on the reader: every one of us ought to suspect himself the more when the question touches his own gain, lest the same covetous desire take away all difference between just and unjust, between what is filthy and what is honest.
26:
Demetrius calls his hearers as witnesses to what has been happening, and in doing so becomes a witness himself. Gill notes the appeal to two senses at once — they could see what was going on in their own city and had heard the report from elsewhere. Barnes calls the sentence the noble testimony of a heathen to the zeal and success of Paul's ministry, an acknowledgement from an enemy that his labours had been strikingly successful in turning people from idolatry; Clarke says the same, that from the mouth of this man we have in one sentence a most pleasing account of how God had blessed the work.

The extent claimed is worth testing, and the grammatical-historical witnesses test it. Ellicott allows that the language may betray the exaggeration of alarm, but holds that it confirms Luke's own earlier statement about all Asia hearing the word; and he sets beside it a letter written half a century later, in which Pliny reports deserted temples, neglected worship, and hardly a single purchaser to be found for sacrificial victims. Robertson agrees that there may be some exaggeration meant to stir the workmen, but treats the sentence as a real tribute to Paul's power as a preacher, and puts the commercial fact plainly: Paul had cut the nerve of their business. He adds a comparison that measures the difference: a Jewish colony had long existed at Ephesus, and its protest against idolatry had amounted to nothing beside the effect of this preaching.

Robertson notes the contempt in the demonstrative — this Paul — and the tense of the last clause, which describes gods being made from time to time, as in a workshop. That, he thinks, is where the sting lay for the men in the room: Demetrius was jealous of the brand of gods his own factory turned out, and the charge was a reflection on their workmanship. The Old Testament had said the same thing far more sharply, in Isaiah's picture of a man warming himself at half a log and worshipping the other half (Isaiah 44:9-17), and Paul had put the point in the same terms at Athens (Acts 17:29).

What the objection concedes is the last thing the witnesses take up. Ellicott observes that the wrath of a mob-leader has made him commit himself to the opposite proposition — that the idol simply is the god. Philosophers might talk of symbolism and ideal representation, but this has always been the conclusion of popular idolatry, and it is being stated here by a man with every motive not to state it. Wesley draws the same inference, that the contrary opinion evidently prevailed in general, namely that there was a real divinity in the sacred images. Chrysostom, hearing the speech as a whole, is struck by how nearly it argued the other way. The very things Demetrius said were enough to bring his hearers to true religion — for if one man could turn away so many, and the worship of the gods stood in jeopardy from him, they might have paused to ask how great this man's God must be.
27:
Demetrius adds a second count, and Barnes points out the order in which the two come. The loss of business is named first, which is what strikes the mind of a man moved by self-interest alone; the danger to the worship of Diana is named second. On the verb Robertson and Ellicott agree that it is stronger than set at nought suggests: literally to come to an exposure, a censure, a rejection after examination — to become, as Ellicott puts it, a laughing-stock and a by-word. Robertson's comparison is domestic: their business of making gods would lose caste as the liquor trade has done in our own day, and they felt it in their pockets. Gill puts the commercial logic in a sentence — who will buy the shrines once men believe there is no divinity in them?

On the goddess herself the witnesses supply what the sentence assumes. Clarke insists she is not the Diana of the hunt at all: covered with breasts from shoulder to foot, crowned with the tower of Cybele, attended by the lions of Cybele, the fruits and oxen of Ceres, the griffins of Apollo, she is a composite figure under whose name nature — the nourisher of all things — was worshipped, as an inscription on two of her images says outright, naming her the mother of all. That is why she is called great, in contrast with the huntress. Ellicott notes that the adjective was specially appropriated to the Ephesian Artemis and appears on the city's coins; Robertson reports an inscription calling her the greatest god, and describes the establishment around her — eunuch priests, virgin priestesses, temple-sweepers, and orgiastic processions. Barnes traces the temple through its several burnings, including the one on the night Alexander was born by a man who confessed under torture that his only motive was to make his name immortal, and ends where a traveller in his own century had to end, with the site no longer identifiable among the ruins.

The claim about the extent of the worship is checked rather than accepted. Robertson calls all Asia and the world an exaggeration, but a pardonable one, since Pausanias says no deity was more widely worshipped and temples of Artemis have been found as far away as Spain and Gaul; Ellicott takes the world in its conventional sense of the Roman empire and quotes Apuleius using almost the same words. Wesley grants the reach and denies that it settles anything: the multitude of those who err does not turn error into truth. His comment on the last clause is the sharpest line in the section — miserable majesty, which was capable of being thus destroyed.

Calvin attacks the order of the speech. Nothing is more absurd than to prefer the belly to the goddess, and Demetrius takes thought for religion only after his trade; had he suffered no loss he would have sat quietly at home. To cover the shame of the thing he cloaks it in the plausible title of religion — and no other witness is needed to refute him, since he cuts his own throat with his own words by betraying first the grief he felt for his own loss. Calvin then names the appeal to numbers as the common refuge of superstition. That all the world worships her is what men plead when they dare not cast off an error because it is everywhere received, setting the very name of custom against God. True religion needs a steadier support than the will of men: the rule prescribed is to be content with God's authority alone, without regard to the opinion of men, our own advantage, or the custom of nations. Ellicott, meanwhile, notices something unintended in the speech: panic is sometimes clear-sighted in its forecasts, and the silversmith of Ephesus has become an unconscious prophet of what actually happened.
28:
The response is a chant rather than an answer. Ellicott and Robertson both read the tense as continuous — they went on crying out, and kept it up — and Robertson adds that such reiteration was characteristic of the orgiastic exercises, so that what the crowd fell into was a form they already knew. Ellicott thinks the cry was probably the usual chorus of the festivals of Artemis, taken up now with the stress falling on the adjective: great she was, whoever might attack her greatness.

Robertson supports that from the epigraphic record. The inscriptions show this to have been the votaries' habitual shout in their processions, an ejaculatory outcry or prayer rather than an argument, and one manuscript preserves it without the article, in the barer and more natural form — Great Artemis of the Ephesians. A similar cry is recorded elsewhere of Apollo. What makes this occasion different, he notes, is that the artisans were not simply worshipping; they were making an argumentative protest, and had chosen a liturgical formula to make it with. The same manuscript adds a detail the others omit, that on hearing Demetrius they ran out into the street — which is plainly what happened next.

Barnes reads the outburst as a tactic rather than a devotion. They were greatly enraged, probably at the prospect of losing their gains, and the design of the clamour was to raise a persecution against Paul and so secure the continuance of their employment. From that he draws two observations, and neither is confined to Ephesus: that when men have no arguments they raise a clamour, and that when their livelihood is threatened they discover a great zeal for religion, expecting by noise on behalf of some doctrine to protect an interest of their own. Gill notes only that the sayings had their effect on masters and workmen alike, which is the point of Demetrius' having gathered both into one room.

What the shout does not contain is any reply to what was actually said. Paul's proposition, as Demetrius reported it, was that things made with hands are not gods; the answer to it is the assertion, repeated at volume, that this particular thing made with hands is very great indeed. Nobody in the theatre appears to notice.
29:
The disorder spreads faster than any account of its cause. Gill pictures the workmen running through the streets with the cry, bringing people out of their houses to ask what the matter was, and the crowd growing as it went. Robertson takes the noun to mean a pouring together, like a flood, and the verb for the rush as an ingressive aorist of impetuous dashing — mob psychology, he calls it, a body of men vociferating the city's watchword. Ellicott supplies the rumour that would have done the work: that the company of strangers, already objects of curiosity and suspicion, were conspiring against the worship that was the city's pride; and he compares the panic at Athens over the mutilation of the Hermae on the eve of the Sicilian expedition.

Where they went is a detail worth explaining, and three witnesses explain it the same way. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all note that a Greek theatre was not merely a place of entertainment but the ordinary venue for public assemblies, courts and elections; Clarke quotes Tacitus on Vespasian addressing the people in the theatre at Antioch, where it was the custom to hold consultations, and a second instance from Agrigentum. Ellicott calls the theatre at Ephesus the city's chief glory after the temple and puts its capacity at twenty-five thousand; Robertson, working from the excavated ruins, reports estimates ranging from about that figure to more than twice it. Both note what such buildings were chiefly used for — combats with wild beasts — and Wesley draws the inference that the mob may have hoped to make the two men fight for their lives there.

The two who were seized are known from elsewhere. Barnes identifies Gaius as the Corinthian who had housed Paul, though Ellicott, counting four men of that common Latin name in the New Testament, keeps the Macedonian of this verse distinct from him. On Aristarchus they agree: a Thessalonian, a Jewish convert, who appears later among Paul's companions on the journey to Jerusalem and afterwards shared his imprisonment at Rome (Colossians 4:10). Ellicott adds that the phrase describing them as Paul's companions in travel implies a missionary activity reaching well beyond the walls of Ephesus, in which they had shared. Robertson admits that how the mob laid hands on these two rather than on Paul is unknown, and offers a guess worth weighing: Paul lodged with Priscilla and Aquila, of whom he afterwards wrote that they laid down their own necks for his life, and it is possible the crowd came to that house and was refused.

Clarke states the cause of the whole scene without any softening: the peace of a great city was disturbed, not by an apostle preaching the gospel, but by one interested and unprincipled man who did not so much as plead conscience for what he did. Calvin looks past the individual to the crowd, which Luke has painted here as in a picture — a city on fire in a moment, and a tempest not easily stilled once raised. His counsel to Christ's servants is that they arm themselves with invincible constancy and not be troubled as at some new and strange thing when they see a people unquiet; and his comfort is that the Lord holds the helm, and is governor of the storms as well as of the church, so that we sail a tempestuous sea and are not suffered to be wrecked. He notes too what the scene shows about crowds: sedition is confused, and yet the people unerringly take the worse part.
30:
Paul's first instinct is to go in, and no witness treats that as reckless. Gill supposes he meant to preach — to remove their prejudice against the gospel, to show them the error of their worship, and to persuade them to do his companions no harm — and finds in it the greatness of the man's soul, his firmness and intrepidity, and his affection for his friends, that he would risk his life so. Barnes says the same more soberly, that he wished to address the people and defend his own cause. Robertson is blunt: Paul plainly wanted to face the howling mob, and was not the man to leave his comrades in the lurch.

Ellicott catches the two pressures in the sentence at once — the impetuous zeal that would not let Paul leave his companions to bear the attack alone, and the anxious fear of friends who saw that his going would endanger his own life without helping theirs. He also thinks this is probably the scene Paul had in mind in speaking of having fought with beasts at Ephesus (1 Corinthians 15:32): not that there was any real prospect of that form of martyrdom, but that a multitude in fanatical rage was as formidable an ordeal; and he notes that Ignatius used the same word of himself, calling the soldiers who guarded him on the road to Rome his ten leopards.

Robertson finds the resistance in the grammar. The verb is what he calls a negative imperfect, denoting resistance to pressure: the more Paul insisted on going, the more firmly the disciples refused to agree — and they won. That is the only outcome the verse records, and it is recorded without apology on either side.

Calvin reads the episode as a lesson in the pairing of two virtues that are usually opposed. Paul's constancy is plain, since he might well have kept himself out of sight and instead offered himself to the danger of his own accord; had he not been held back, what he intended could not have been charged to rashness, for he had not caused the sedition and had reason to hope for a good outcome. But when the brethren, who knew the state of affairs better than he did, dissuaded him, he did not stand stoutly by his own purpose — and it is his modesty in that, Calvin says, that deserves commending. Wesley puts the same courage more plainly: he was above all fear, and meant to plead the cause of his companions and to prove that they are not gods which are made with hands.
31:
A second and more surprising intervention comes from the officials of the province. Who the Asiarchs were the witnesses take care to establish, since the older English titles mislead. Gill objects to rendering them princes or chief men of Asia at all: they were not civil magistrates but presided over the games and the diversions of the theatre, and he cites as an instance Philip the Asiarch in the account of Polycarp's martyrdom, whom the crowd begged to loose a lion on the old bishop, and who answered that he could not, the theatrical exercises being over. Barnes and Clarke describe them as a kind of high priest, charged with the public games and with seeing that proper honour was paid to the emperor at the festivals; Barnes adds that they were annually elected, that their election was confirmed at Rome, and that they held a common council in the chief city of the province. Ellicott and Robertson put their number at ten, chosen from the leading cities, the proconsul naming one of them as president, and note that only rich men could serve, since the games were financed out of their own pockets — for which reason the office was eagerly sought.

Why they were in Ephesus at that moment Ellicott explains from the calendar, and the explanation ties the whole riot together. If the letter Paul was then writing was written about Passover, the tumult falls in the spring, in the month named after the goddess herself, when the great festival was being kept or expected — which is both why the Asiarchs were in the city and why the populace was more than usually open to an appeal like the silversmith's.

That such men were Paul's friends is the detail every witness pauses on, and they divide over what it means. Clarke says flatly that they could not have been Christians, though they were what the text calls them, his friends. Barnes agrees that nothing here shows them to have been converts, but supposes they had heard him preach during their stay and were favourably disposed. Robertson goes a little further, holding that they evidently thought highly of him and were at least tolerant toward his preaching, and recalls that it was an Asiarch at Smyrna who resisted the cry to throw Polycarp to the lions. Ellicott draws the general point out of it: the manliness, tact and courtesy that tempered Paul's zeal seem always to have won him the respect of men in authority — Sergius Paulus, Gallio, Festus and Agrippa, the centurion Julius — and here they win him the protection of the very men who ran the festival he was preaching against.

Their message agrees with the disciples' judgement, and Robertson reads the imperfect as showing that the messengers had to press it over Paul's objection. The idiom rendered adventure himself means literally to give himself, and is the phrase used elsewhere of Christ giving himself for our sins; here it marks a hazard, and Robertson's estimate of it is short — the theatre was no place for Paul, and would have meant certain death. Clarke, having said as much, cannot resist a question he leaves unanswered: did he go in after all, and was that the fighting with beasts he afterwards spoke of?
32:
Luke's description of the crowd is the one every witness stops to admire. Barnes calls it an admirable account of a mob assembled for a purpose it did not know, agitated by passion and strife; Clarke says the same of men gathered without law or reason, their passions inflamed and looking for an occasion to commit outrages without why or wherefore. Robertson reads the imperfect as continuous — they kept on crying — and the periphrastic pluperfect behind was confused as describing a settled state rather than a moment, so that what stood in the theatre was not an assembly at all but a wholly disorganised mob. Wesley notes only that the ignorance of the greater part is commonly the case in such a gathering.

The word Luke chose for that gathering is the point Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all fasten on. It is ecclesia, the very word the New Testament uses for the church — which shows, Clarke argues, that the term of itself means simply an assembly, good or bad, lawful or unlawful, and that only the circumstances can determine which. Ellicott notes that the recorder will presently draw exactly that distinction himself, since strictly this was no lawful assembly, though the word had come to be used loosely; and Robertson thinks Luke's choice of it here, immediately qualified by the word for confusion, is a mark of contempt for what he is describing.

Ellicott finds in the vividness of the whole passage an argument about its source. Narrative of this graphic quality is almost certain to have come from an eyewitness — and Aristarchus and Gaius, who were in the middle of it, afterwards travelled with Luke and were with him at Rome. He allows himself one further guess, following his earlier conjecture about the owner of the lecture hall: Tyrannus may have written the whole account of the tumult and sent it to Luke. He also observes that the connecting particles at the head of the verse carry the reader back inside the theatre, after the parenthesis about what had been happening outside it between Paul, the disciples and the Asiarchs.

Gill guards the sentence against a misreading, noting that the disagreement described is not among the disciples over whether Paul should go in, but among the people in the theatre, who could not agree on what the trouble was about. Robertson notices who is missing from the account: Demetrius, who raised the mob and is known to be its ringleader, has now chosen to stay in the background. Henry draws from the scene the plainest of rules — not to be hasty or rash in our motions, but to take time to consider, and to keep our passions in check.
33:
A man is pushed to the front, and almost every question about him is open. Barnes admits that who this Alexander was is not known, and reports Grotius' identification of him with the coppersmith who did Paul much harm (2 Timothy 4:14) without endorsing it. Gill and Clarke both accept that identification, Gill adding that though the name is Greek it had become common among the Jews since the time of Alexander the Great. Calvin thinks the conjecture allowable, and if it is the same man draws a hard lesson from it: let us learn by so fearful an example to walk circumspectly, since one who stood here at the point of martyrdom afterwards became a treacherous apostate.

Whose cause he was to plead is the sharper question. Barnes corrects the older translation on this very point — the Greek says he was about to make a defence, not his, since he was not personally accused; what he meant to defend was the Jews in general, who could see that the heathen took the Christians for a Jewish sect and were about to be blamed for a tumult they had not caused. Clarke agrees, and adds the likely reason for the choice: Alexander was probably an able speaker, and there is no ground in the text for supposing him a Christian. Ellicott reads the Jews' anxiety the same way, as a wish to guard against being identified with Paul, and suggests that if the coppersmith is meant, a trade connection with Demetrius would explain his influence with a crowd of artisans. Robertson puts the fear plainly — some of the Jews saw that a mob roused against Christians might turn on Jews as well, Paul being a Jew and Aristarchus another — and recalls that Alexandria had already seen disgraceful scenes of that kind.

Two witnesses read the scene in the opposite direction. Wesley takes Alexander for a well-known Christian whom the artificers saw in the crowd, and thinks the Jews thrust him forward to expose him to the greater danger. Calvin holds much the same: the Jews did not send him out to plead the nation's cause but to have him brought before the people and murdered — and he barely escaped with his life as it was.

What actually happened is described with a precision nobody misses. Robertson notes the old verb for shaking the hand rapidly up and down to win a hearing, and the imperfect that follows: he wanted to make a defence, started to, and apparently never got a word out. Ellicott paints the same moment — the vain attempt to gain a hearing by signs and gestures, and then the fury of the people the instant they recognised his Jewish features and dress, together with their ready assumption that every Jew abhorred their images. He adds an uncomfortable possibility about what else they may have suspected, since Paul himself asks elsewhere whether men who abhor idols nonetheless rob temples (Romans 2:22) — and the recorder's own words a few verses later suggest the same thought was in the air.
34:
Recognition takes only a moment. Robertson and Ellicott both note that the verb means a full and immediate recognising, and Robertson supposes it was the man's features that gave him away at sight. Gill puts the crowd's reasoning in a sentence: a Jew was equally an enemy of their worship, whether he was a Christian or not. Barnes explains the confusion behind that, since the heathen took the Christians for a sect of the Jews and were therefore indiscriminate in their wrath, unwilling to hear any defence at all.

What follows is the one moment in the chapter when the whole crowd agrees. Robertson catches the grammar of it — one voice arose from all of them crying — and observes that the unanimity Demetrius had failed to produce by argument arrived instantly at the sight of a Jew about to speak. Their creed, he says, is contained entirely in that prolonged yell, the same cry with which the disturbance had begun. Barnes gives the duration its due: the ancient hour, being a twelfth of the day from sunrise to sunset, was not materially different from ours, and it is not at all improbable that two hours were needed before such an excitement could burn itself out. He also distinguishes the two purposes it served — first to silence Alexander, and then to display their attachment to Diana. Wesley says it in a phrase: they prevented him.

Calvin weighs the shout as a confession of faith, which is what it formally is, and finds it hollow. It was clamorous enough, but without soundness, and it did not proceed from the faith of the heart; the greatness of Diana came from nothing but the fury with which men defend an error once received. True godliness runs the other way about — we believe with the heart unto righteousness, and the confession of the mouth follows unto salvation — and that order is precisely what distinguishes the constancy of the martyrs from the stubbornness of brain-sick fools.

Then Calvin turns the comparison against his own readers, and it is the sting in the verse. Our sluggishness is shameful if we are not as ready and as stout in confessing a certain faith as these men were in confessing a filthy error. The Spirit of God has prescribed the rule by the mouth of David: I believed, therefore have I spoken (Psalms 116:10). Two hours of shouting for a thing that is not true is a rebuke to anyone who cannot manage two minutes for a thing that is.
35:
The man who finally quiets the theatre is not what the English title suggests. Robertson explains that Ephesus was a free city electing its own officers, and that the recorder was its chief magistrate — not a copyist, but the most influential man in the place, who drafted the decrees, controlled the assembly, and dealt directly with the proconsul. Ellicott, who calls him the keeper of the city's records, points out that since his office was probably permanent while the Asiarchs' lasted a year, he carried more weight with the people. Gill and Clarke both object to the older rendering as far too small. Robertson adds the detail that makes the scene work: he took the rostrum, waited until the shouting had nearly exhausted itself, and only then began.

Ellicott's estimate of the speech itself is the shrewdest thing said about it. The language of a public officer is as characteristic in its grave caution as the silversmith's had been in its brutal frankness. He plainly regards Paul and his companions with respect and would not willingly be a persecutor; but he dares not oppose the multitude, and so soothes them with a loud profession of attachment to the religion of his country. He was, Ellicott says, the Gamaliel of Ephesus — the kind of man who appears in every critical time of religious change, holding the balance between contending parties.

The two titles he gives the city are technical, and the witnesses explain both. The word rendered worshipper means literally temple-sweeper, and Barnes and Clarke are careful to say that this was no humble office: among the ancients the keeping of a temple was a post of honour, and the men who held it offered sacrifices for the life of the emperor. Whole cities took the title, and Ephesus was proud of it above all others; Robertson cites a coin of the year 65 describing the city in exactly Luke's words, and Ellicott quotes an inscription claiming for it the honour of being the goddess's nurse — she was, he says, to borrow a phrase whose analogy is only too painful, Our Lady of Ephesus.

The second title concerns the image, believed to have fallen from the sky. Every witness reads that belief the same way: the thing was so ancient that no one knew who had made it or when, and a heavenly origin filled the gap — as it did for the Palladium of Troy and the sacred shields of Numa. Clarke passes on an ugly explanation from Isidore of Damietta, that the artists who made such images were banished or killed so that no evidence of their making should survive. Ellicott and Barnes both allow that a meteoric stone may lie behind the story. Wesley detects a purpose in the recorder's raising it at all: if the image fell from Jupiter, it was not made with hands, and so was not the kind of idol Paul had said was no god.

Calvin refuses to be charmed. The tumult was appeased, but superstition still prevailed and the truth of God was not heard; the recorder, as politic men do, counted it enough to quiet the crowd, and to do it he extolled the feigned power of Diana and maintained her worship. Had Paul been in the theatre he would have died a hundred times rather than be delivered at that price, since to keep silence while such an excuse was made would have been treacherous dissimulation in a public witness of heavenly doctrine. Which is why, Calvin says, Luke took care to record that the brethren kept him out. Barnes ends on the recorder's confidence: he thought the worship of Diana too well established for a few Jews to shake, and little knew that the religion he was dismissing would overturn not only her temple but the whole splendid idolatry of Rome.
36:
The argument the recorder builds on his premises is prudential rather than religious, and the witnesses say so. Robertson notes that the adjective rendered cannot be spoken against is a rare verbal form meaning undeniable, and observes drily what is being called undeniable: the legends were accepted as true, and they appeased the mob. Gill takes the intention to be reassurance — these things are so certain that nobody would attempt to contradict them, and therefore the crowd must have mistaken the men they had dragged in. Barnes lays out the syllogism: since nobody can question the zeal of the Ephesians, and since there is no danger that a worship so well established will be destroyed by a few Jews, there is no occasion for a tumult at all.

Ellicott hears something else in the tone. The language has the ring of an official acceptance of the established cult rather than of any strong personal devotion, and such language, he notes, has often been heard from the defenders of institutions that were nearly at the point of ruin. In the exhortation to do nothing rashly he hears the voice of a worldly prudence — partly Gamaliel again, partly the maxim of a modern statesman that what one wants above all is no zeal.

On the two verbs at the end the comment is chiefly linguistic and chiefly practical. Barnes points out that be quiet translates the same word used a verse earlier of the recorder himself quieting the people, so that he is asking them to do for themselves what he has just done for them; Robertson gives the same participle in the perfect, a settled calm rather than a momentary one. The adjective behind rashly means literally falling forward, headlong, precipitate, and Robertson's gloss on it is a proverb: better look before you leap.

Henry takes the sentence out of the theatre altogether and makes it a rule of life. It is a very good rule at all times, in private affairs and public alike, not to be hasty and rash in our motions, but to take time to consider, and always to keep our passions under check — to do nothing in haste of which we may repent at leisure. That the advice comes from a pagan official defending a superstition does not spoil it; it may even be the point. The man who stops the riot does so by telling an inflamed crowd to think before acting, and the counsel is good whatever the creed of the man giving it.
